lede: CSV is how data arrives; Parquet is how most pipelines keep it. A columnar file stores the schema with the data, so types survive, files are smaller and Spark can read just the columns a query needs.
objectives: Write a DataFrame as Parquet and read it back with its types intact
Explain what's inside a Parquet folder: part files, compression and a `_SUCCESS` marker
Write and read ORC, the other common columnar format
Avoid the error from writing to a folder that already exists

blocks.md:
`trips` has one row per taxi ride: times, zones, distance, and money columns as exact decimals. It was read from CSV with a schema, which is the only reason those columns have types at all: the CSV file itself is just text.

`df.write.parquet(path)` saves a DataFrame in Parquet format. Every example here writes under `/tmp`, the one place the course's Spark can write, and adds `.mode("overwrite")` so it can run again. `spark.read.parquet(path)` reads it back.

blocks.title: Write Parquet, read it back
blocks.note: No schema was given to the read, yet every column comes back with its type: timestamps, whole numbers, a double and `decimal(8,2)` money. Parquet keeps the schema inside the file.

blocks.md: Compare that with a round trip through CSV. Written as CSV and read back without a schema, every column is text again, and you'd have to repeat the schema on every read.

blocks.title: The same round trip through CSV
blocks.code:
trips.write.mode("overwrite").csv("/tmp/taxi/trips_csv", header=True)
trips.write.mode("overwrite").parquet("/tmp/taxi/trips")

as_csv = spark.read.csv("/tmp/taxi/trips_csv", header=True)
as_parquet = spark.read.parquet("/tmp/taxi/trips")
print(dict(as_csv.dtypes)["fare"], dict(as_csv.dtypes)["pickup_at"])
print(dict(as_parquet.dtypes)["fare"], dict(as_parquet.dtypes)["pickup_at"])
blocks.note: From CSV, `fare` and `pickup_at` are strings; from Parquet, they're still a decimal and a timestamp.

blocks.md:
The path you write to is a **folder**, not a file. Inside it:

- one or more `part-...` files hold the rows, one per partition of the DataFrame being written. Their names include a random id, so never rely on them.
- an empty `_SUCCESS` file marks that the whole write finished.
- small hidden `.crc` files hold checksums.

Parquet files are compressed. The default codec is `snappy`, which is fast; the `compression` option picks another, such as `gzip`. The codec shows in the file names.

Because Parquet stores each column separately, a query that selects two columns reads only those two from disk. On wide tables that's the biggest saving of all.

blocks.title: What's in the folder
blocks.code:
import os

trips.write.mode("overwrite").parquet("/tmp/taxi/trips")
files = sorted(os.listdir("/tmp/taxi/trips"))
print(len([f for f in files if f.startswith("part-")]), "part file,", "_SUCCESS" in files)
print(sorted({f.split("c000")[-1] for f in files if f.startswith("part-")}))

trips.write.mode("overwrite").option("compression", "gzip").parquet("/tmp/taxi/trips_gzip")
gz_files = os.listdir("/tmp/taxi/trips_gzip")
print(sorted({f.split("c000")[-1] for f in gz_files if f.startswith("part-")}))
blocks.note: Twelve rows from one small file make one partition, so there's one part file. Its name ends in `.snappy.parquet`; with `compression="gzip"` it ends in `.gz.parquet`. Plain Python's `os.listdir` lists the folder; the code prints only what doesn't change between runs.

blocks.md: **ORC** is the other columnar format you'll meet, common in Hive-based platforms. It works the same way: `df.write.orc(path)` and `spark.read.orc(path)`, with the schema stored in the file. Its default compression here is `zstd`.

blocks.title: ORC keeps the schema too
blocks.code:
import os

trips.write.mode("overwrite").orc("/tmp/taxi/trips_orc")
orc = spark.read.orc("/tmp/taxi/trips_orc")
print(sorted({f.split("c000")[-1] for f in os.listdir("/tmp/taxi/trips_orc") if f.startswith("part-")}))
print(orc.dtypes == trips.dtypes)
orc.select("trip_id", "trip_distance", "total", "payment_type").show(3)
blocks.note: Same columns, same types, same values as the original `trips`.

blocks.md: Without a mode, a write refuses to touch a folder that's already there. That protects data from being replaced by accident. `.mode("overwrite")` replaces the folder's contents; the lesson on write modes covers the others.

blocks.title: Writing to a folder that exists
blocks.note: The first line creates the folder; the second has no mode, so it stops rather than replace what's there. The error names the path and suggests `mode("overwrite")`.

concept.prompt: You write `trips` to Parquet and read it back without a schema. What type is `fare`?
concept.why: Parquet stores the schema with the data, so types come back exactly as they were written.

choices: A folder with part files and a `_SUCCESS` marker
A CSV file with a Parquet header
concept.why: Spark writes a folder: one part file per partition, plus `_SUCCESS` when the write finished.

concept.prompt: What happens if you run `trips.write.parquet(path)` when `path` already exists?
choices: It adds the rows to the folder
It fails with an error, because no mode was given
It writes to a new folder next to it
concept.why: The default refuses to write to an existing path. Use `.mode("overwrite")` to replace it on purpose.

review: `df.write.parquet(path)` writes Parquet; `spark.read.parquet(path)` reads it back with its schema, no options needed.
Parquet and ORC are columnar: types survive, files are compressed, and Spark reads only the columns a query selects.
A write produces a folder of `part-` files (random names) and a `_SUCCESS` marker.
Parquet compresses with `snappy` by default; `option("compression", "gzip")` picks another codec.
`df.write.orc(path)` and `spark.read.orc(path)` work the same way for ORC.
Writing to an existing path fails unless you choose a mode such as `.mode("overwrite")`.
